title: The Idiot, Part 2
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
summary: Na primeira parte, o bondoso príncipe Míchkin se apaixonou por duas mulheres, viu Nastássia Filíppovna fugir com Rogójin e quase foi morto pelo próprio "irmão" numa escada escura. Agora, no verão de Pávlovsk, entre passeios no parque, concertos e intrigas da alta sociedade, o príncipe se aproxima da orgulhosa Aglaia, enquanto Nastássia Filíppovna e Rogójin continuam rondando sua vida. O jovem tuberculoso Ippolit, condenado à morte pela doença, lê em voz alta uma confissão desesperada, e as duas mulheres caminham para um confronto que vai decidir o destino de todos.

chapters.title: Summer in Pavlovsk
paragraphs: Lebedev's summer house in Pavlovsk was small but pretty, with a wide terrace covered in climbing plants and a little garden full of flowers. The prince spent his first days there lying on a sofa, weak from his fit, watching the green light through the leaves. The town was full of rich families from Petersburg, and every evening the music from the bandstand in the park drifted through the warm air.

On the third day, the whole Yepanchin family arrived on the terrace. Lizaveta Prokofyevna had heard that the prince was ill, and she had come in a state of great agitation, convinced that he was dying. When she found him sitting up and smiling, she was almost angry.

“So you're not on your deathbed at all!” she cried. “And I came running like a fool. Well, I'm glad. Sit down. Don't get up. Why didn't you come to us when you arrived? Six months, and one stupid letter!”
“I didn't think you would want to see me,” said the prince.
“Nonsense. You're one of the family.”

The three girls came in behind her, with Prince Shch., who was engaged to Adelaida, and a tall, handsome, elegant man of about twenty-eight, Yevgeny Pavlovich Radomsky. Everyone said that he was going to marry Aglaya. He was rich, clever, and ironical, and he looked at the prince with polite curiosity.

Later, when the others were busy, the general took the prince aside. “A word, my dear fellow,” he murmured, looking around. “You know who has taken a house in Pavlovsk this summer? She has. Nastasya Filippovna. She drives about in a carriage, and everyone stares. My wife is beside herself. Be careful, Prince. Be very careful.”
Kolya, who was now often at the Yepanchins', began to laugh about something. “Aglaya Ivanovna,” he said, “tell the prince about the poor knight.”

Aglaya blushed deeply. “It's nothing,” she said. “Kolya is being silly. There's a poem by Pushkin about a poor knight, who saw a vision of the Virgin and devoted his whole life to her. He never looked at another woman again, and he wrote her initials on his shield in his own blood. I said once that the prince was like that knight. That's all.”
“Read it to us,” said Lizaveta Prokofyevna. “I don't know it.”

Aglaya stood up in the middle of the terrace and recited the poem. She read beautifully, with great seriousness, but when she came to the initials on the shield, she did not say “A.M.D.”, as Pushkin wrote. She said, quite clearly, “N.F.B.”

The prince turned pale. Everyone understood at once: Nastasya Filippovna Barashkova. Lizaveta Prokofyevna looked from her daughter to the prince and back again, completely confused. Yevgeny Pavlovich smiled.
“What a strange choice of initials,” he murmured.

“I did it on purpose,” said Aglaya calmly. “The knight in the poem loved an ideal. He didn't care whether she loved him or not. He believed in her, and he would have died for her. That's a great thing. I meant it seriously, and nobody here understands anything.” And she sat down.
The prince looked at her and did not know whether she was praising him or mocking him. Probably, he thought, she did not know herself.
At that moment Lebedev came hurrying in with an anxious face. “Prince, there are some young men here to see you. They've been waiting since morning. They say it's a matter of honour.”
“Let them come in,” said the prince. “I'm not hiding from anyone.”
“Yes, let them come in,” said Lizaveta Prokofyevna, sitting back in her chair. “I want to see these young men. I'm not leaving.”

chapters.title: The Son of Pavlishchev
paragraphs: Four young men came onto the terrace. The first was Antip Burdovsky, a sullen young man of about twenty-two, badly dressed, who kept his eyes on the floor. Beside him was a nephew of Lebedev's, Doktorenko, a student with a loud, aggressive voice. Then there was Keller, a retired lieutenant and a boxer, who had been one of Rogozhin's band. And the fourth was a boy of seventeen or eighteen, thin and pale, with fevered eyes and red spots on his cheeks. This was Ippolit Terentyev, Kolya's friend, who was dying of consumption.

They sat down without being invited, and Doktorenko began. “Prince, we have come to demand justice, not to ask for charity. This is Burdovsky, the son of the late Nikolai Andreyevich Pavlishchev, your benefactor. Pavlishchev paid for your treatment in Switzerland. He spent thousands on you, a stranger, while his own son lived in poverty. Now you have inherited a fortune. Honour demands that you give Burdovsky what is his.”
“We do not ask,” added Ippolit, “we demand.”

Then Keller produced a newspaper and read aloud an article which he himself had written. It was a coarse and comic attack on a certain “idiot prince” who had been raised on charity, had inherited millions, and refused to pay his debts to his benefactor's son. The prince listened with growing embarrassment. Lizaveta Prokofyevna's face became redder and redder.

When it was over, the prince spoke quietly. “Gentlemen, I believe that Mr. Burdovsky is acting in good faith, and that he has been deceived. I asked Gavrila Ardalionovich to look into this matter a week ago. I was ready to give Mr. Burdovsky ten thousand roubles, not because I owe it, but because Pavlishchev was kind to me. Ganya, would you explain?”

Ganya, who had arrived with Varya and Ptitsyn, stepped forward and explained very calmly. He had found Burdovsky's mother and made inquiries. Burdovsky had been born too late; Pavlishchev was abroad at the time. He could not possibly be his son. Pavlishchev had once loved Burdovsky's mother's sister, and he had helped the family out of kindness. Lebedev's nephew and a clever lawyer had invented the whole story.

Burdovsky turned purple. “I didn't know,” he muttered. “I believed it. I won't take your money. I don't want it!” He threw an envelope on the table. Inside was the money that the prince had sent him the week before. Then he paused, confused. Lebedev pointed out with delight that a hundred roubles were missing from it.
“I spent it on my mother,” Burdovsky said. “I'll pay it back.”
“It doesn't matter,” said the prince quickly. “Forgive me, I didn't mean to humiliate you. Gentlemen, I offer you my friendship. If Mr. Burdovsky ever needs anything—”
“You see?” cried Ippolit, laughing. “He's offering us his friendship, as if we were children! He's trying to buy us. How noble! How Christian!” He began to cough terribly and had to stop.

Lizaveta Prokofyevna could bear it no longer. She jumped up. “Enough! This is madness! You,” she said to the prince, “you'll be asking them to forgive you next. You'll be begging them on your knees. And you,” she turned to the young men, “are you not ashamed? A sick, half-witted man, and you come to rob him in the name of justice! And this boy,” she pointed to Ippolit, “a dying child, they've brought him here to shout about rights, instead of putting him to bed!”

Ippolit stared at her in astonishment. Then, suddenly, his face crumpled. “Excuse me,” he said, and he began to tremble. “I'm going to die in two or three weeks. The doctor told me. I wanted to look at people and trees before I die. You're right to call me a child.”
Lizaveta Prokofyevna looked at him, and her face softened completely. “You poor thing,” she said. “Sit down. Drink some tea. You must stay here tonight.”

chapters.title: A Voice from the Carriage
paragraphs: The quarrel seemed over. Ippolit was drinking tea, and the others were making ready to leave. But Ippolit could not stop talking. In a feverish voice he told everyone that he had wanted to live, that he hated everyone for being alive and healthy, and that he had a plan for his last days.
“I'll tell you all one day,” he said, smiling strangely. “I'll read you something.”
“You'll go to bed,” said Lizaveta Prokofyevna.

At last the Yepanchins rose to leave. Yevgeny Pavlovich offered his arm to Aglaya, and they were all walking down the steps into the road, when a magnificent open carriage drawn by two white horses came racing past and stopped just beside the house. In it sat two ladies, beautifully dressed. One of them leaned forward and called out in a clear, ringing voice:
“Yevgeny Pavlovich! Is that you? I'm so glad I found you! Don't worry about those IOUs. Rogozhin has bought them all up for me. You don't need to worry about them any more. I've arranged everything!”
Everyone froze. The voice belonged to Nastasya Filippovna. Before anyone could answer, the carriage drove off at full speed. She looked back once, laughing.
Yevgeny Pavlovich was pale. “I have no idea what she means,” he said, with a forced smile. “I've never had any dealings with that lady. I don't understand.”

But the damage was done. Lizaveta Prokofyevna stared at him coldly. Everyone knew that IOUs meant debts, and that a man in debt to a moneylender like Rogozhin was not a desirable husband for Aglaya. The family walked home in icy silence.
The prince stood on the terrace, shaken. He understood that Nastasya Filippovna had done this on purpose. She wanted to ruin Yevgeny Pavlovich in Aglaya's eyes. She wanted Aglaya to marry the prince.

Later that evening, Keller, the boxer who had written the newspaper article, came back alone and asked to speak to the prince privately. He wanted to confess everything. He told the prince how he had lied and cheated, how he had written the article for money, and how he had always been weak.
“And now,” said Keller, “I'll be honest with you. I came to confess, but I also came to borrow a hundred and fifty roubles. Both thoughts were in my head at the same time. Isn't that disgusting?”
The prince laughed gently. “Not at all. Everyone has these double thoughts. I have them myself all the time. You can't judge yourself too harshly for them. They come by themselves. Here's the money.”

Keller left, astonished. Then Lebedev came in and confessed the same thing: he had helped the young men with their plan, and now he was sorry. The prince forgave him too. He was beginning to understand that in Pavlovsk he would be surrounded by people who wanted to use him.
The next morning, Lizaveta Prokofyevna came alone to the prince's terrace. She sat down heavily and looked him straight in the eye.
“Tell me honestly,” she said. “Did you write a letter to Aglaya in the spring?”
“Yes,” said the prince. “Only a few lines.”
“Show me what you wrote. No, don't. I believe you. But tell me, why her? Why not to me, or to Alexandra? Why to Aglaya?”
“I don't know,” said the prince. “I wanted very much to write to her. That's all.”

Lizaveta Prokofyevna looked at him for a long time, and then she sighed. “She keeps it,” she said. “She keeps it hidden in a book. I found it by accident. Oh, Prince, you'll be the death of me, and you don't even know what you are doing.”

Two days later, Yevgeny Pavlovich came to see the prince. His uncle, he explained, had shot himself in Petersburg after stealing government money, and the family fortune was gone. The IOUs did exist, but he did not know how Nastasya Filippovna had got hold of them.
“She wants to harm me,” he said. “And I think I understand why. She wants you to have Aglaya.”
The prince did not answer.

chapters.title: The Scene at the Bandstand
paragraphs: A few days later, the prince met the Yepanchins in the park in the evening. It was the hour when all of fashionable Pavlovsk came to listen to the orchestra at the bandstand. Ladies in light summer dresses walked arm in arm under the lime trees, officers bowed and smiled, and children ran around the flowerbeds.

Aglaya was in an odd mood. She walked beside the prince, and she was cheerful one minute and silent the next. Suddenly she said, without looking at him, “Do you think I'm going to marry Yevgeny Pavlovich?”
“I don't know,” said the prince. “Everyone says so.”
“Everyone is stupid,” said Aglaya. “I'll never marry anyone here. I want to run away from home. I want to go abroad and study, and do something useful. Would you help me?”
“Of course,” said the prince, astonished.
“Then you're my only friend,” she said, and she laughed. “But don't imagine anything. You're not the kind of man one marries.”

Before he could answer, there was a stir in the crowd. People were turning to look at someone coming along the path. It was Nastasya Filippovna. She was dressed magnificently and walked with a group of noisy young men, and she was laughing loudly. Several ladies quickly led their daughters away.

She stopped right in front of the Yepanchins and looked straight at Yevgeny Pavlovich. “Well, well!” she cried. “Haven't you heard? Your uncle, Kapiton Alexeyevich, has shot himself! This morning! He stole three hundred and fifty thousand roubles of government money. Didn't you know? Everyone knows.”

Yevgeny Pavlovich went pale but kept his composure. A young officer who was with him, a friend of his, said loudly in French, “She ought to be whipped! That's the only way to deal with creatures like her.”
Nastasya Filippovna heard him. She turned like a flash. In the hand of a young man passing by she saw a thin riding whip. She snatched it and struck the officer across the face with all her strength.
There was a shout. The officer, beside himself with rage, rushed at her with his fists raised. But the prince, who was standing nearby, seized his arms from behind and held them.
“You can't do that!” the prince said. “She's a woman. She's ill. She doesn't know what she's doing.”

The officer pushed the prince violently away, and he fell against a chair. At that moment Rogozhin appeared out of the crowd. Without a word, he took Nastasya Filippovna by the arm and led her quickly away. As he went, he turned to the officer and said with a mocking smile, “Calm down, sir. You've been hit by a lady. If you want satisfaction, find me. I'm Rogozhin.” Then, to the prince, he said in a low voice, “Thank you for that.”

The crowd broke up. Lizaveta Prokofyevna was so angry that she could not speak. She took her daughters and marched home. But Aglaya, as they left, turned and gave the prince a look that he could not understand, a look full of excitement, almost of joy.

That evening, the officer sent a friend to tell the prince that he expected a duel. Keller, who had heard everything, came running to offer to be the prince's second. The prince laughed. “I'm not afraid of a duel,” he said, “but I'm sure that no one will fight. We'll all drink champagne and become friends.” And indeed, the next day the officer sent word that he considered the matter closed.

But late that night, as the prince sat alone, a servant girl brought him a note from Aglaya. It said: “Do not come to see us for a while. I have something important to say to you. Tomorrow morning, at seven o'clock, wait for me at the green bench in the park. You know which one. Tell no one. And don't think that I am in love with you.”

The prince read it over and over. Then he began to laugh, very quietly, with a happiness he had never felt before. He put the note away and walked up and down the terrace until it was very late. The music in the park had long since stopped. The sky was pale with the white night of the north.
“My God,” he thought, “what's happening to me?”
Just then, in the shadows by the garden gate, he thought he saw a dark figure watching him. When he looked again, it was gone.

chapters.title: The Prince's Birthday
paragraphs: The next evening was the prince's birthday. He had told no one, but somehow everyone knew, and by nine o'clock his terrace was crowded. Lebedev brought out champagne. Kolya came, and Keller, and Burdovsky, who had apologized and become one of the prince's admirers. Ganya and Ptitsyn came. General Ivolgin came, in his best coat. Yevgeny Pavlovich arrived late, calm and amused. And Ippolit came too, wrapped in a coat although the night was warm, coughing and feverish.

The conversation grew lively. Lebedev, drunk on his own champagne, began to explain the Book of Revelation and to argue that the railways were destroying the soul of mankind. “There's no unifying idea any more!” he cried. “In the Middle Ages, people ate each other during famines, it's true, but they had an idea, an idea stronger than hunger. Show me an idea today that binds mankind together!”
Yevgeny Pavlovich laughed and argued with him. The prince listened with pleasure. Then, a little after eleven, someone else appeared at the foot of the terrace steps. It was Rogozhin.
He had come to congratulate the prince. The two men went aside into the garden and talked quietly for a while. The prince told him plainly that he forgave him for the staircase.

“I knew you'd say that,” said Rogozhin, not looking at him. “But I don't forgive myself. I wanted to kill you, Lev Nikolayevich. I'd been thinking about it for weeks. And it wasn't her, it was you. Don't trust me. And remember, she loves you, not me.”
“Let's not talk about it,” said the prince. “Today is my birthday. Come and sit with us.”
They went back to the terrace. Ippolit, who had been drinking champagne and growing more and more excited, suddenly stood up. He took out of his pocket a large envelope sealed with red wax.

“Gentlemen,” he announced. “I have something to read to you. It's called ‘My Necessary Explanation’, with the epigraph: ‘Après moi le déluge’, after me the flood. I wrote it last night. I want you all to hear it. It concerns my death.”
“It's late,” said someone.
“It won't take long,” said Ippolit, with a twisted smile. “Forty minutes, perhaps an hour. Prince, may I?”
The prince looked at him with sadness and nodded. Ippolit broke the seal with trembling fingers. The guests settled down, some curious, some bored, some uneasy. Rogozhin sat in a corner, very still.
“‘Yesterday morning,’” Ippolit began, “‘the prince came to see me.’” His voice was hoarse, and he read quickly, nervously, stopping often to cough. And soon the terrace was completely silent.

He told them how, a month before, the doctor had told him he had only a few weeks to live. From that moment he had looked at everything differently. From his window he could see a great dirty brick wall, the wall of a house that belonged to a man called Meyer. “I have looked at Meyer's wall for six months,” he read, “and I know it better than any face. I hate it. It has told me everything.”

He told them of a poor doctor he had helped, a man who had come to Petersburg to look for a position and had found nothing. Ippolit had picked up the man's lost wallet in the street, returned it, and later, through a relative, had found the doctor a job. He told it with pride and with shame. “So I did one good deed,” he read. “Do you know that there is something tempting in a good deed? You plant a seed, and you never know what will grow from it. I understood then that I could have spent my life sowing seeds. But I have no life.”

chapters.title: Ippolit's Explanation
paragraphs: Ippolit went on reading, and the night grew paler around them.

He described a dream he had had. In his room there appeared a horrible creature, like a scorpion but bigger and uglier, brown, with a hard shell, crawling quickly across the floor and up the walls. His mother and a big black dog, Norma, were with him. The dog attacked the creature and caught it in her teeth, and the creature stung her tongue. The dog stood trembling, and Ippolit woke up.

Then he described the picture he had seen in Rogozhin's house. “I visited Rogozhin once,” he read, and several people looked at the silent figure in the corner. “He showed me a painting, the dead Christ taken down from the cross. Looking at that body, broken and decaying, you think: if death is so terrible, if the laws of nature are so powerful, how can they be overcome? How could the people who loved Him, who stood around Him, believe, looking at that corpse, that He would rise again? Nature appears in that picture like a huge, deaf, merciless machine, which has seized and crushed and swallowed a great and priceless being, a being worth all of nature and all its laws.”

Then he told them of a strange night. Very late, he said, he had woken up and seen Rogozhin sitting silently in a chair in the corner of his room, looking at him with a mocking smile. Rogozhin had sat there for a long time without speaking, and then he had got up and left. Ippolit did not know whether it was a dream or real. The door had been locked.
At this, Rogozhin spoke for the first time. “It wasn't me,” he said quietly. “I've never been to your room.”
“I know,” said Ippolit. “That's why I decided to die.”

He read the end quickly. Since nature had condemned him to death in a few weeks, he would not wait for nature. He would choose his own moment. He would kill himself, to be free, to show that he was still master of something. “I will die looking at the rising sun,” he read. “I want to leave this world with dignity. I do not need your forgiveness. Nobody will be guilty. I only want you, the living, to know that I have seen everything and that I refuse.”

He put down the papers. He was white, and drops of sweat stood on his forehead. Nobody moved. Then, just as the edge of the sun appeared above the trees, there was a burst of loud and nervous laughter. Ferdyshchenko had arrived during the reading, and he was mocking. Others began to argue. Lebedev said that the boy should be watched. Someone said the whole thing was nonsense, a show.
“So you think I'm only pretending?” said Ippolit. “Ha!” He turned away and walked to the end of the terrace, near the steps. Everyone saw him take something out of his pocket.
Before anyone could stop him, he raised a small pistol to his temple and pulled the trigger.
There was a click. Nothing else. Ippolit stood for a second with the pistol pressed to his head. Then he fell into Keller's arms in a faint.
Keller took the pistol and examined it. “The cap!” he said. “He forgot to put the percussion cap in! The pistol couldn't fire.”

For a moment there was silence. Then somebody began to laugh. Soon half the guests were laughing loudly, nervously, at the boy who had tried to shoot himself and forgotten the cap. When Ippolit came to his senses, he heard the laughter. He sobbed and grasped the prince's hand.
“I didn't forget,” he gasped. “I swear I didn't! It's a terrible accident. Now they'll say I'm a coward, that I did it on purpose. Prince, believe me!”
“I believe you,” said the prince gently. “I believe you completely. Nobody thinks you're a coward. You must sleep now.”

They carried Ippolit into the house and laid him on the sofa. Rogozhin left without a word. The guests drifted away. At last the prince was alone on the empty terrace, where the bottles stood among the plates and the morning birds were beginning to sing.

He thought of Ippolit, and of the young man's question: how can anyone believe, looking at the body of the dead Christ? He thought of the wall outside the boy's window. He remembered his first months in Switzerland, when he too had felt like a stranger at a great feast, a feast that went on and on and had no end, where every little fly knew its place and was part of the chorus, and only he was alone and did not belong. He had wept then, in the mountains, as Ippolit was weeping now.
Then he remembered that it was nearly seven o'clock. He had an appointment at the green bench.

chapters.title: The Green Bench
paragraphs: The green bench stood in a quiet corner of the park, under the trees, not far from the Yepanchins' house. The prince sat down on it and, exhausted by his sleepless night, fell asleep almost at once.

He dreamed of a woman. He knew her face, and the knowledge was painful. It was Nastasya Filippovna, and yet she seemed like a criminal who had just committed a terrible crime. She was looking at him and beckoning him to follow her, with her finger on her lips. He woke up with a start. Aglaya was standing in front of him, laughing.
“You're asleep! You fell asleep waiting for me!”
“I didn't sleep all night,” said the prince, jumping up. “Forgive me.”

She sat down beside him. She had heard all about Ippolit and the pistol from Kolya. Then she grew serious. “I asked you here,” she said, “because I want to make you my friend. I want to talk with you as I'd talk with myself. Do you know that everyone in my family thinks I'm in love with you?”
The prince blushed.

“They're wrong,” she went on quickly. “But I respect you more than anyone. You have the chief mind, the mind that matters. The others don't. I want to run away from home with your help. I'm tired of my family. They want to marry me off. I want to be useful. I've already asked you; you said you'd help me.”
Then, abruptly, she asked, “Is it true that you lived with that woman in Moscow for a month?”
“It's true,” said the prince sadly. “But not in the way you think. I'll tell you everything, Aglaya Ivanovna.”

And he told her. He told her about Nastasya Filippovna's suffering, about her endless self-punishment, about how she believed herself guilty and fallen, and how this conviction gave her a terrible, unnatural pleasure. He told her that she had run away to him and then back to Rogozhin, because she thought he would be ruined if he married her.
“I loved her,” he said. “I loved her very much. But now I can't look at her face. I'm afraid of it. She's mad, Aglaya Ivanovna. I'm sure of it. And she writes to you. Doesn't she?”
Aglaya looked at him in astonishment. “How do you know?”
“I guessed. She wants you to marry me. She's arranging it all, like a game.”

Aglaya took out of her pocket three letters and showed them to him. They were written in a fine, nervous hand. In them, Nastasya Filippovna wrote to Aglaya as if to an angel. “You are perfect,” she wrote. “You are innocent, and he loves you. Marry him. When you are married, I will marry Rogozhin. Don't think of me. I have already gone. Rogozhin keeps a razor in a drawer, wrapped in silk, I think. I don't care.”

The prince read them and went cold. Aglaya watched his face. “These letters are insane,” she said. “She's in love with you herself. She writes to me that she loves me, but she means that she loves you. She wants me to be her sacrifice.”
“Yes,” said the prince quietly. “She's in love with me. And she'll destroy herself.”

Aglaya stood up abruptly, flushed with anger. “Then go to her! Go and save her. Go and marry her. Why should I care?” She stopped. “No. Forgive me. I didn't mean that. Listen. Do you see that I've chosen you?”
The prince stared at her, unable to speak.
“Not to marry!” she cried, laughing and blushing. “Don't be stupid. To be my friend. Goodbye.”
She ran off through the trees. The prince stayed on the bench a long time. He felt that his heart was too full, and that he would never understand anything again.

chapters.title: The Hedgehog
paragraphs: That night, as the prince walked in the park, he met Nastasya Filippovna. She appeared suddenly out of the darkness, alone, in a light dress, and fell on her knees in front of him on the path.
“Are you happy?” she asked in a whisper. “Are you happy? Tell me just that one word. You were with her today, at the green bench. What did she say?”
“Get up,” said the prince, trying to raise her. “Please, get up.”

She seized his hands and kissed them. “I'm going away tomorrow. You won't see me again. I'm saying goodbye forever. Be happy. Marry her. And don't think of me.” Then Rogozhin came up from the shadows and led her away, gently and silently, as if he were leading a child. As they went, she looked back at the prince over her shoulder.
“Look,” said Rogozhin, “she's going. She'll never marry me until she sees you married to the other one. That's the deal. Do you understand now?”

The next morning, the prince did a very strange thing. In the market he bought a small hedgehog from two schoolboys, and he had it sent to Aglaya in a basket, with a note. When Aglaya received it, she was delighted. She sent Kolya to ask the prince a most important question: was the hedgehog intended as a joke, or as a symbol of deep respect?
“Neither,” said the prince, confused. “I just saw it and thought she would like it.”
When Kolya told her this, Aglaya laughed and was perfectly happy. The family did not know what to make of it.

In the following days, everything in the Yepanchin house seemed to turn around the prince. Aglaya treated him in public with mockery and contempt. She called him an idiot, laughed at everything he said, and told everyone she would never marry such a ridiculous man. But every evening she wanted him to come, and if he was late, she was in a bad temper. Lizaveta Prokofyevna watched, worried and puzzled. “She's in love with him,” she said to her husband. “God help us. With the idiot!”
“He's a prince, and he's rich,” said the general cautiously.
“He's a holy fool,” said his wife. “And she'll make his life a misery. But I like him. Oh, I don't know what to think!”
One evening at tea, with the whole family present, Aglaya suddenly said in a loud, clear voice: “Prince, I want to ask you a serious question. Are you asking for my hand or not?”
The tea cups froze in the air. The prince turned red. “I... yes,” he stammered. “Yes, I am. I love you. I want to marry you, Aglaya Ivanovna.”
“Are you rich?” she asked, quite seriously. “What is your income? How will you support a wife?”

The prince, bewildered, began to answer her questions honestly, giving numbers and figures. Then Aglaya looked at her mother and sisters and burst into wild laughter. Everyone began to laugh, even the general, and the prince laughed too, happily, not knowing why.
“There, you see,” said Aglaya, still laughing. “I've done what I wanted. Now he's asked, and I'll never marry him. Never!” And she ran out of the room.
But later that evening, when the prince was leaving, she came out to him on the stairs. She took his hand. “Forgive me,” she whispered. “I'm a horrid, spoiled girl. Forgive me for laughing.”
“I'm the happiest man in the world,” said the prince.
She looked at him with tears in her eyes. “Then you will come tomorrow?”
“Of course.”
“And you won't think of that woman any more?”
He could not answer that question as quickly as the others, and she saw it. Something darkened in her face, but she said nothing more. She only pressed his hand and went upstairs.

Some evenings Aglaya made him play chess with her. She was a good player and beat him easily, and she was so delighted that she laughed at him for an hour. Then she suggested a simple game of cards, and to her fury the prince won every single game. She threw the cards on the table, went upstairs, and refused to come down again. The next day she sent him a note asking him to forget the whole matter, and to come early.

Ippolit, who was still staying with Lebedev, had been watching all this with bitter amusement. He was growing weaker every day, but he did not want to die any more. One morning, he said to the prince, “You think I'm a dying boy who doesn't understand. But I'll tell you something. Aglaya will make you suffer. And Nastasya Filippovna will make you suffer more. You're like a man standing between two fires. And you'll be burned.”
“Perhaps,” said the prince calmly. “Tell me, Ippolit, how do you think I should die? What is the best way?”
Ippolit stared, then laughed. “You're a strange man. Pass by us, Prince. Pass by and forgive us our happiness. That's how you should live.”

chapters.title: The Chinese Vase
paragraphs: At last Lizaveta Prokofyevna decided that the prince must be introduced to society. The engagement was not yet announced, but everyone in Pavlovsk was talking about it. One evening the Yepanchins gave a party for a few important guests: an old princess, a great dignitary, a famous poet, and other people of high standing. The prince was to be presented to them.

Aglaya was terrified that he would disgrace himself. The day before, she told him, half seriously, half laughing, “Tomorrow, don't talk about anything clever. Don't wave your arms. And don't break anything. There's a great Chinese vase in the drawing room. Mother values it more than anything. If you break it, I'll never speak to you again.”
The prince promised to sit quietly and say nothing. He went home convinced that he would break the vase.

At first everything went well. The guests were kind and polite, and the prince was charmed by them. He thought he had never met such gracious, sincere people. He told himself that all he had heard about the coldness of the aristocracy was untrue. Then one of the old gentlemen mentioned that Pavlishchev, the prince's benefactor, had become a Roman Catholic before his death, under the influence of a Jesuit priest.
The prince was deeply upset. He began to speak, quietly at first, then more and more passionately.

“Catholicism is worse than atheism!” he said. “Atheism only preaches nothing, but Catholicism preaches a distorted Christ. It has sold Christ for earthly power. Atheism came out of Catholicism, and so did socialism, out of despair. We must show the West our Russian Christ, whom they do not know! The Russian soul will save the world!”

Everyone stared at him. He was waving his arms. Aglaya was looking at him with terror. He saw her face, he remembered the vase, and at that very instant his arm struck the great Chinese vase on its stand. It swayed for a second, then crashed to the floor and broke into pieces.

There was a cry. The prince stood frozen, looking at the pieces with horror. But then the old gentlemen laughed kindly, and Lizaveta Prokofyevna said, “Never mind, never mind, it doesn't matter.” Everyone was so friendly that the prince was overcome with gratitude.

He began to speak again, even more passionately, about how beautiful they all were, about how a man could be happy just by looking at a tree, about how the aristocracy should not die but be reborn. “I'm afraid you all think I'm ridiculous,” he cried, “but I'm not ashamed. I'm not afraid of being ridiculous. How can one walk past a tree and not be happy to see it? How can one speak to a man and not be happy to love him?”
He stood up. His face was strange, his eyes shining. Aglaya ran to him. He looked at her with a radiant smile, and then a terrible scream burst from his chest, and he fell to the floor in a fit.
When the guests had gone, the general said sadly, “Well, that's settled. He can't marry Aglaya. He's an invalid.”
“He's a good man,” said Lizaveta Prokofyevna, crying. “The best man I've ever known. But you're right.”

Aglaya said nothing that evening. The next day she sent word that she wanted to see the prince. When he came, pale and weak, she told him that she did not care about the party or the vase or what people said.

“I'll never marry you,” she said fiercely, “but I want you to come with me this evening. I'm going to see Nastasya Filippovna. I want her to tell me to my face what she wants from us. And you must come.”
“I'll come,” said the prince. He did not try to argue.

chapters.title: Two Women
paragraphs: They walked there in the warm evening without saying a word. Aglaya walked quickly, her lips pressed together, and did not look at him once. The prince felt that something terrible was going to happen, and that he could not stop it. Once he tried to speak, but she silenced him with a gesture.
“Don't talk,” she said. “Not now. Afterwards you can say whatever you like.”

Nastasya Filippovna was staying in Pavlovsk in a small wooden house belonging to Darya Alexeyevna. When Aglaya and the prince arrived, she was waiting for them in the drawing room. She wore a plain dark dress, and her face was very pale. Rogozhin was there too, sitting in a corner like a shadow, silent and watchful.

The two women looked at each other for a long moment. Neither of them sat down at first. Then Nastasya Filippovna smiled and invited Aglaya to take a chair, and they sat facing each other, with the prince between them.
“You wrote to me,” Aglaya began, her voice trembling with anger. “You had no right to write to me. I came to tell you that.”
“Is that all you came to tell me?” said Nastasya Filippovna softly.

“No,” said Aglaya. She looked at her rival with all the pride and hatred of her nineteen years. “I came to tell you what you are. You wanted to be an angel to him, a sacrifice. You were dishonoured by Totsky, and you decided to play the part of a fallen angel. You wanted to make the prince suffer, and to make me feel grateful to you. If you had really loved him, you would have left him alone. You wouldn't write me letters. You'd have married Rogozhin long ago, or gone to work like an honest woman, or gone to a convent. But no, you prefer your own misery. You love your shame. That's the truth.”

Nastasya Filippovna went white. “And you,” she said, in a strange, quiet voice, “why did you come here? To see if I'm still more beautiful than you? To see if he loves me more than you? You came because you were afraid of me.”
“I'm not afraid of you!” cried Aglaya. “I despise you!”

“Then why did you come? You came because you know he still loves me.” Nastasya Filippovna stood up. Her eyes were blazing now. “Do you want me to call him? Do you want me to tell him to leave you and stay with me? I can do it, you know. One word from me, and he'll stay. Do you want to see?”
Aglaya was trembling. She had not expected this. She had come to win, and suddenly she was afraid.

“Go away, Rogozhin!” cried Nastasya Filippovna, turning wildly to the corner. “Get out! I don't need you!” Then she turned to the prince, her face full of despair and madness. “Look, Prince! Choose! Is she to go, or am I? Choose now! Is it her or me?”

The prince looked at the two women. He saw Aglaya's frightened, proud face. Then he looked at Nastasya Filippovna, at her wild eyes and white lips, at the pain in her face that he had seen in her portrait on the first day. He could not bear it.
“How can you?” he said to Aglaya, his voice full of reproach. “Don't you see how unhappy she is? Look at her! She's mad!”

That was all. He had only spoken out of pity. But Aglaya looked at him with a look of such suffering that he would remember it for the rest of his life. She covered her face with her hands and cried, “Oh, my God!” and ran out of the room.
The prince ran after her, but at the door Nastasya Filippovna threw her arms around him. “You're going after her? After her!” she screamed, and she fell unconscious in his arms.
He carried her to the sofa. He knelt beside her and stroked her hair and her face, like a child's. Rogozhin stood watching them for a minute.
“So,” he said, with a dark smile. “Now it's yours. Goodbye.” And he went out.

When Nastasya Filippovna opened her eyes, she saw the prince beside her. She laughed and cried at the same time. “He's mine!” she whispered. “He's mine! Aglaya's gone, and he stayed with me. He's mine!” She clung to him and would not let him go.

The prince sat with her all night, stroking her head, comforting her. He did not think of himself at all. He thought only that he could not leave her now, that she would die if he left. But he also kept seeing, in his mind, the look on Aglaya's face as she ran out.

The next morning, he went to the Yepanchins' house. He was not admitted. Lizaveta Prokofyevna sent word that Aglaya was ill and could not see anyone, and that he was not to come again. The servants looked at him coldly. Even Kolya avoided him in the street.
Within a few days, all Pavlovsk knew. The prince was going to marry Nastasya Filippovna. The wedding would be in two weeks.

chapters.title: Yevgeny Pavlovich's Verdict
paragraphs: A week later, Yevgeny Pavlovich came to see the prince. He had been a frequent visitor at the Yepanchins', and now he came, he said, as a friend.

“Prince,” he began, “I want to speak to you frankly. What you did that evening was cruel. You had a girl who loved you, a proud, pure girl, the best girl in the world, and you abandoned her in the most humiliating way, in front of her rival. She'll never recover from it.”
The prince listened with his head down. “I know,” he said. “I know. It was my fault.”

“Let me finish. I'll tell you what I think happened. You came from Switzerland, a strange, innocent young man, full of ideas. The first thing you saw in Petersburg was a beautiful woman, abused and wronged, and you fell in love with your own idea of saving her. You were intoxicated by the chance of being a hero, a knight. You loved a principle, not a woman. You fell in love with her suffering, not with her. Isn't that true?”
“Perhaps,” said the prince, very low. “Perhaps you're right.”
“And Aglaya? Did you love her?”
“Oh, yes!” cried the prince. “Yes, I love her! I love her with all my heart.”
“Then how can you marry the other one?”

The prince looked at him with great distress. “I can't leave Nastasya Filippovna,” he said. “You didn't see her face. If I leave her, she'll die. You don't know. She's a child. She's been wounded all her life. I can't. And I can love Aglaya and still marry her. I don't know how to explain it.”
“So you'll love both of them?”
“Yes. Yes, both of them.”

Yevgeny Pavlovich stood up and looked at him with deep pity. “My poor prince,” he said. “What a strange man you are. Do you know what everyone is saying? That you're an idiot after all. I don't think so. But I fear for you. You don't know what you're doing.”
“Tell Aglaya,” said the prince, “that I would give anything to see her for one minute, only to explain.”
“I'll tell her. But she won't see you.”

When he had gone, the prince sat alone a long time. He thought of Aglaya, and he could not believe that he would never see her again. He thought of the wedding. He did not feel joy, only a strange, heavy calm.

Nastasya Filippovna, meanwhile, was in a fever of activity. She ordered dresses, flowers, carriages. She wanted the wedding to be grand. But at night she was seized by fits of terror. She would wake up screaming that Rogozhin was in the garden, that he was hiding in the house, that he would kill her. Sometimes she would look at the prince and burst into tears, saying she was ruining him. Then she would laugh and talk about the future. Darya Alexeyevna told the prince that she was not sleeping.

Ippolit, who was now very ill, enjoyed all of this with a kind of malice. One day he said to the prince, “Do you know, Rogozhin came to see me. He asked me about the wedding. He was very calm. Too calm. I wouldn't let your bride out of your sight, Prince.”

General Ivolgin, too, came to a sad end in those days. He had stolen four hundred roubles from Lebedev, and when he was found out, and Lebedev forgave him in a humiliating way, he could not bear the shame. He had a stroke in the street and died a few days later. The prince stayed by his bedside until the end, and Kolya wept in the prince's arms.
“You're the only one who was kind to him,” said Kolya. “You never called him a liar.”

On the day before the wedding, the prince walked past the Yepanchins' house. The windows were closed, and the family had left for Petersburg. As he stood there, he remembered the green bench, the hedgehog, the laughter at the tea table. It all seemed as far away as Switzerland.

chapters.title: The Wedding Day
paragraphs: The wedding was fixed for eight o'clock in the evening, at the little church in Pavlovsk. Since early morning a crowd had been gathering in the street outside Darya Alexeyevna's house. The whole town was curious. People had come from Petersburg just to see the famous beauty marry the idiot prince. Some were laughing; some were indignant. Some said openly that the bride ought to be hissed.

Keller was to be the prince's best man, and he was extremely proud of the honour. He had wanted to bring a group of friends to keep order, and even offered to fight anyone who insulted the bride, but the prince had begged him to keep calm. Lebedev, who had been plotting against the marriage for days and had even tried to persuade a doctor to declare the prince insane, now ran around giving orders as if he had arranged everything himself.

The prince himself was quiet and serious. All day he had been calm, almost happy, though Kolya noticed that he looked often towards the window. At about half past seven, he went ahead to the church with Keller. The church was full. People were standing on the steps and in the street outside.

At the house, Nastasya Filippovna was being dressed. She had been in a feverish state all day. In the morning she had wept and said she was a wicked woman who was ruining the prince. In the afternoon she had laughed and admired her dress. Now, as her maids fastened her veil, she looked in the mirror and became very still. Then she asked anxiously, again and again, whether Rogozhin was in the crowd.
“No, no, he's not here,” said Darya Alexeyevna. “Calm yourself.”

Her dress was magnificent, white and silver, and her hair was dressed with flowers. When she came out onto the steps, the crowd fell silent for a moment, astonished by her beauty. She was pale as death, but her eyes were shining. Then a few people began to laugh and whistle. Someone shouted something rude. Others shouted back.
“What a beauty!” said a voice. “She'll make a fine princess.”
“A princess! She's been everybody's but she's never been a princess!”

Nastasya Filippovna paused on the steps, ready to get into the carriage that was waiting. And then, suddenly, she saw him. Standing at the edge of the crowd, a little apart from the others, was Rogozhin. His eyes were fixed on her.
She gave a cry. She went down the steps and rushed through the crowd like a madwoman, straight to him. She seized both his hands.
“Save me!” she cried. “Take me away! Anywhere you like, now!”

Rogozhin almost lifted her in his arms. He carried her to a carriage that stood waiting nearby, as if he had expected this, pressed a hundred-rouble note into the driver's hand, and shouted, “To the station! If you catch the train, there's another hundred for you!” He jumped in after her, and the carriage galloped away down the street.

The crowd was stunned for a few seconds, and then burst into a storm of noise. Some were laughing, some shouting, some running after the carriage. Keller arrived at the church first, out of breath, to tell the prince.
The prince listened. He grew a little pale, but he did not seem surprised. “In her state,” he said quietly, “it was only to be expected.”

He went back to Lebedev's house and sat down calmly on the terrace. Keller and Kolya and Lebedev stood around him, waiting for him to break down. He did not. He only asked for tea. Later, some people from the crowd came up to the terrace to stare at him, and some of them even broke the glass of the windows. He seemed not to notice. Later still, Kolya found him sitting alone in the dark, with his face in his hands, and he did not say a word.

At last, around midnight, he went to bed. Lebedev told Kolya in a whisper that it was a great relief, and that God had saved the prince from a terrible marriage. Vera, Lebedev's daughter, went quietly to the prince's door to listen. She heard him moving about the room. She heard him say, aloud, “Rogozhin,” and then nothing more.
In the morning, the prince took the first train to Petersburg. He told no one where he was going, but Vera Lebedeva, who had come to bring him tea, saw his face and was frightened.
“You're going to look for her,” she said. “Prince, be careful.”
“I'll come back,” said the prince. “I promise.” And he went.

chapters.title: The Gloomy House
paragraphs: It was about ten o'clock in the morning when the prince reached Petersburg. He went straight to Gorokhovaya Street, to Rogozhin's house. He rang at the door of Rogozhin's apartment. For a long time nobody answered. Then an old servant opened the door and said that Parfyon Semyonovich was not at home.
“Not at home since yesterday?” asked the prince.
“He's not at home,” said the woman, and she looked at him strangely. “He hasn't been here. I don't know when he'll come back.”

The prince went upstairs to see Rogozhin's mother, but she was asleep, and the servants would not let him in. He came out into the street and looked up at the windows. He had the strong impression that one of the curtains had moved, as if someone had looked out and quickly stepped back. But he could not be sure.

He went to the house where Nastasya Filippovna used to stay in Petersburg, with a German lady she knew. The German lady had not seen her for weeks. Nobody had seen her. The prince went from one place to another all day, asking, waiting, coming back to Gorokhovaya Street. He rang Rogozhin's bell again and again, and each time he was told the same thing.
“Strange,” he thought. “In a moment I'll understand everything. I'm about to understand something.” But the thought escaped him each time.

The day was hot and stuffy, as it had been on that other day, the day of the knife. He took a room in the same hotel where Rogozhin had once waited for him on the stairs, and he even asked for the same room. Several times he went down into the street. Everything seemed familiar and terrible to him: the narrow staircase, the stone pillar, the dark recess on the landing. He felt that his illness was close, that a fit might seize him at any moment.

Once he went to Ippolit's mother, the widow Terentyeva, who had moved back to the city with her younger children, because Ippolit had once said that Nastasya Filippovna had visited them. The widow knew nothing. She offered him tea, and her little boy asked whether the prince had found the lady he was looking for. “Not yet,” said the prince, and he smiled at the child, but his hands were cold.
In the early evening, as he walked along a street near the hotel, someone touched his elbow. He turned. It was Rogozhin.
“Lev Nikolayevich,” Rogozhin said in a low voice, almost a whisper, “come with me, brother. I need you.”
The prince was so astonished and so glad that he did not at once understand. “Parfyon! Where is she? Is she with you?”
“Come,” said Rogozhin. “She's at my house. I was waiting for you. I saw you ring at the door this morning. I was behind the curtain.”
“And she?”
“She's there too. Walk on the other side of the street. Don't walk beside me. We must not be seen together. I'll explain everything.”

They walked through the streets in this strange way, Rogozhin on one pavement and the prince on the other, until they reached the gloomy green house. Rogozhin opened a side door very quietly with his own key, so that the servants would not hear, and they went up the stairs in silence. He let the prince into the apartment and locked the door behind them.

The rooms were dark. The curtains were drawn, and the evening light came in only faintly. Rogozhin did not light a candle. He led the prince through the study, where they had once talked about God and the dead Christ, and stopped in front of a heavy green silk curtain that divided the study from the bedroom.
“Is she there?” whispered the prince.
“She's there,” said Rogozhin.
The prince's heart was beating so loudly that he thought Rogozhin must hear it. He felt that his legs were trembling. He stood looking at the curtain, and he could not move.
“Come in,” said Rogozhin, and drew aside the heavy curtain.

chapters.title: The Night in Rogozhin's House
paragraphs: The bedroom was even darker than the study. A large bed stood at the back of the room, behind another curtain, and on it someone was lying, completely still. The prince could see nothing clearly at first. Then his eyes grew used to the darkness, and he saw that the figure was covered from head to foot with a white sheet. Only the tip of a bare foot could be seen, very white, as if carved from marble.

Around the bed lay scattered things: a white silk dress, flowers, ribbons, a pair of shoes. On a small table by the bed, diamonds were glittering, thrown down carelessly. A fly woke up somewhere, buzzed over the bed, and settled near the head.
The prince stood and looked, and the longer he looked, the more terrible the silence became. He began to tremble.
“Let's go out,” said Rogozhin, touching his arm. “Let's sit down.”
They went back into the study and sat down on two chairs, facing each other. For a long while they said nothing. The prince's whole body was shaking.

“I killed her,” said Rogozhin at last, very quietly. “Last night, after we came back. With the knife, the one you saw on my desk. I didn't take it from her afterwards. It went in so deep, there was hardly any blood. Only half a spoonful. That's strange, isn't it?”
“Yes,” said the prince, and his teeth chattered.

“We came back from the station. We were going to go to Moscow, or to Oryol, I don't know. But she was afraid. She didn't want to go. So we came here. I locked her in. Nobody knows she's here. I covered her with the oilcloth, the good American oilcloth, and I put four bottles of Zhdanov's disinfectant around her, so there won't be any smell. You saw the bottles?”
“I saw them.”

“Listen, Lev Nikolayevich. They'll come, sooner or later. They'll come and they'll take me away. But I don't want them to take her away yet. I want us to stay here tonight, you and I, with her. Together. Let's not tell anyone. Let them come in the morning.”
“Yes,” said the prince. “Yes. We'll stay.”

Rogozhin got up and made a bed on the floor of the study, with cushions from the sofa, near the green curtain. They lay down side by side. It was very quiet. Only the clock ticked somewhere in the dark house.
“Did you have your knife,” the prince asked suddenly, “that day, on the staircase?”

“Yes, I had it,” said Rogozhin. “I'd been carrying it all day. And last night, I knew I would do it. I knew it for a long time. She knew it too. Do you remember? She told you. She said, ‘I know he'll kill me.’ But she came with me anyway.”

The prince did not answer. After a while, Rogozhin began to talk in a strange, broken way, now about the card games they had played in Moscow, now about the people in the crowd at the wedding, now about how she had laughed at him. Sometimes he laughed himself, quietly and horribly. The prince listened, and when Rogozhin cried out or began to shake, the prince stretched out his trembling hand and stroked his hair and his cheeks gently, like a mother soothing a sick child.
“Parfyon,” he whispered once. “Parfyon.”

Rogozhin did not answer. He had begun to rave, muttering words that made no sense. Then he became quiet, then screamed again. The prince lay beside him all night, unable to sleep. He no longer felt his legs. Tears ran down his face, but he did not know he was crying. He went on stroking Rogozhin's hair, softly, patiently, hour after hour.
The night passed. The grey light of morning came through the curtains. Outside, the city was waking up.

At about seven o'clock, the door of the apartment was broken open. Lebedev, Keller and the police had been searching for the prince all night. Darya Alexeyevna had told them that Nastasya Filippovna had disappeared with Rogozhin, and Lebedev, who suspected everything, had gone to Gorokhovaya Street. The servants said that Rogozhin had come home secretly in the night, and that a stranger had been with him.

When they came into the study, they found the two men lying on the cushions. Rogozhin was unconscious, burning with brain fever, muttering and shouting. The prince was sitting beside him, motionless, stroking his head with his hand. He did not recognize anyone. He looked at them without understanding, with an empty, gentle look, and he did not answer when they spoke to him. He was once again the idiot that he had been as a boy, before Switzerland.

chapters.title: What Became of Them
paragraphs: Rogozhin was ill for two months with brain fever. When he recovered, he was put on trial. He confessed everything simply and clearly, and he did not try to defend himself. He did not even allow his lawyer to say that he had been out of his mind. He said he had known exactly what he was doing. The court took his illness into account and sentenced him to fifteen years of hard labour in Siberia. He heard the sentence in silence, sternly and thoughtfully. His enormous fortune, except for a small part spent on his first wild months, went to his brother.

The prince never recovered his mind. Yevgeny Pavlovich, who had been away, came back when he heard the news and took charge of everything. He arranged for the prince to be sent back to Switzerland, to Dr. Schneider's clinic, and he paid for it himself. He visited him there. Dr. Schneider shook his head and said that the prince's mind was now permanently damaged. He no longer understood where he was or recognized his friends. He sat quietly, smiled gently, and looked at the mountains.

Lebedev, Keller, Ganya, Ptitsyn and the other people of Pavlovsk went back to their own lives. Ganya was ill for a long time after the events of that summer; he had been more shaken than anyone expected. Varya married Ptitsyn, and they took care of Kolya, who had become a quiet, serious young man. Kolya wrote letters to the prince in Switzerland, though he knew that they were not understood.

Ippolit died two weeks after the prince was taken away. He had wanted to live until the last moment, and he had talked endlessly of the prince and Rogozhin, as if he envied them. He died in great agitation, still arguing about the meaning of life.

Nina Alexandrovna, Ganya's mother, never got over the death of her husband. Lebedev's daughter Vera wept for the prince for weeks, and she wrote to Yevgeny Pavlovich to ask for news of him. Yevgeny Pavlovich answered her kindly, and some people began to say that there was a growing friendship between them.

As for Aglaya, she did something nobody expected. A few months later, she married a Polish count, a romantic émigré who was said to be a great patriot fighting for his country's freedom. He was neither rich nor a count, as it turned out, and he had no great cause; he was a liar and an adventurer. He took her abroad, quarrelled with her family, and turned her against them. Under his influence and that of a Catholic priest, she was converted to Catholicism, and she joined some sort of foreign committee for the restoration of Poland. Her family hardly ever saw her again.

The Yepanchins went abroad that winter. Adelaida married Prince Shch., and Alexandra remained at home. Lizaveta Prokofyevna went to Switzerland and visited the prince at Dr. Schneider's. She sat with him for a long time and wept bitterly. He did not know who she was, but he smiled at her, as he smiled at everyone.

When she came out of the clinic, Yevgeny Pavlovich was waiting for her. She was furious with Europe, with the foreign doctors, with the Poles, with the bad bread and the cold rooms and the endless rain.

“Enough of these enthusiasms!” she said, wiping her eyes. “It's time to come to our senses. All this, all this life abroad, all this Europe of yours, it's all a fantasy, and we abroad are all a fantasy. Mark my words, you'll see it yourself.”
She looked back once more at the white building among the mountains, where the prince sat by a window, looking out at the snow on the peaks.
“He was the only good man among us,” she said. “And we didn't know what to do with him.”
